Ten Commandments. The foundational moral and religious laws given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai, according to Hebrew scripture. Presented as inscribed on two stone tablets, these commandments form the ethical core of Judeo-Christian tradition, encompassing duties to God and to one's neighbor. They remain one of the most recognizable and culturally influential texts in Western civilization.

They are divided into two categories. The first four address duties to God—worshipping no other gods, not making idols, not misusing God's name, and remembering the Sabbath as holy. The remaining six concern interpersonal ethics—honoring parents and prohibiting murder, theft, false witness, adultery, and coveting.

The Ten Commandments appear twice in the Hebrew Bible—in Exodus and in Deuteronomy—with minor textual variations between the two accounts, reflecting different traditions of transmission through Jewish history.

They are known as the Decalogue from the Greek for "ten words" or "ten sayings," emphasizing their role as foundational divine utterances, the core of divine law revealed at Sinai.

They were placed in the Ark of the Covenant, a sacred container held in the inner sanctum of the Jewish Temple, making them the holiest object in Judaism and the central relic of Israelite worship.

The Ten Commandments have been interpreted and amplified through centuries of rabbinic commentary. Each commandment spawned hundreds of subsidiary laws and debates about proper observance. The Talmud develops vast jurisprudential frameworks from these ten principles.

They were adopted into Christian moral theology and embedded in Western legal systems, from Puritan New England to modern constitutions referencing natural law. Many Western codes trace their ethical foundations to this text.

They have been historically displayed prominently in American courthouses and public spaces, making them a flashpoint in modern debates over secularism, religious freedom, and the role of faith in law.
